Well… memory, I don’t know if it’s memory like forgetting where I put my purse, though that happens some like it does with everybody. But thinking clear, yes, I think that’s part of what people notice. It’s embarrassing to say, but when the ladies at church ask me something simple, like about blankets for the drive or when choir practice is, I mean to just answer them plain.

And then somehow my words sort of… take a side road. I’ll start with the blankets, and then I’m talking about beans, because maybe I was thinking about supper, and then hymns come into it, and then my roses out back, and I can see their faces change. They look at me like they’re trying to follow, but they can’t find where I’m going with it.

It’s not that I’m trying to be difficult. In my head it feels connected for a second, but once it comes out, I can tell it didn’t land right. And then I get flustered, which makes it worse, because I try to explain what I meant and it just gets more tangled. So yes, around those times, I guess I do have trouble thinking clear enough to say things the way I mean them.

I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I still care about church and my family, if that’s what you mean. I don’t feel like I just stopped loving those things. But sometimes I don’t feel as eager to go and do as much, especially if I think I might get mixed up or people might notice me not answering right.

So I don’t know if that’s losing pleasure exactly, or if it’s more that I get nervous and tired thinking about it. I’ll still like seeing people once I’m there, usually, but getting myself ready and deciding to go can feel like a bigger thing than it used to.

As for appetite and sleep… I can’t say I’ve noticed anything real clear. Some nights I sleep better than others, but I think that’s been true for a long time. And eating, well, I eat. Some days I don’t feel like fixing much, but I wouldn’t say there’s been some big change that I can point to. I’m sorry, I know that’s not a very straight answer.

It seems to come and go some, I think… but it’s been happening enough these past months that I notice it more, especially when people ask me things at church.

Like, if the ladies ask me something simple — “Are the blankets in the closet?” or “Are you coming to choir practice?” — I mean to answer just that. I really do. But then my words sort of run off without me. I’ll start about the blankets, then somehow I’m talking about beans from the potluck, then a hymn we used to sing, then my roses at home, and I can see on their faces they’re trying to follow me but they can’t find what I’m saying.

It’s not that I’m trying to be difficult. In my head it feels like the pieces are connected, but when they come out of my mouth, they don’t line up right. Some days it’s not as bad, if I’m calm and nobody is rushing me. But other days, especially when I feel put on the spot, I just can’t seem to stay on the one thing they asked.

Yes… that’s the trouble I notice. When the ladies at church ask me something simple, like whether the blankets are in the closet or if I’m coming to choir practice, I really do mean to answer them plain. I know what they asked me, at least at first.

But then once I start talking, it’s like my words take a side road. I’ll begin with the blankets, and then somehow I’m talking about the beans from the potluck, and then that reminds me of a hymn, and then I’m saying something about my roses at home. In my mind it feels tied together somehow, like one thing leads to the next, but I can see by their faces that they’re not following me.

They’ll just look at me kind of puzzled, like they can’t find the point of what I’m saying. And then I get embarrassed, because I wasn’t trying to wander all over. I was only trying to answer the question.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
No… I don’t think so. Not like that.

I mean, I might lose track of what I was doing in the middle of something, or I might have to think a minute what day choir practice is, but I don’t usually forget where I am or who people are. At church I know I’m at church, and I know the ladies there. I know my family when they come around.

Sometimes if I’m tired or somebody asks me too many things at once, I can feel mixed up, but it’s more like I need a minute to gather myself. I haven’t had anybody say, “You don’t know where you are,” or anything like that. At least… not that I know of.

I think… it’s hard for me to say if it’s worse every month, like in a straight line. It hasn’t been like one day I was fine and then the next month I couldn’t do anything. But it has gotten to where I’ve had to step back more than I wanted to.

It can happen even when I think I’m all right, Doctor. That’s part of what scares me, because I won’t always feel mixed up beforehand.

Most days I’m just… trying to get through what I’m supposed to do.\n\nI wouldn’t say I’ve been unusually up or elated. At my age I’m not exactly bouncing around anyway. And sad… well, I get embarrassed and worried about those things happening, and that can sit heavy on me, but I haven’t noticed some big change in my mood, not like you’re asking, I don’t think.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or sounds that others couldn't hear, or felt that people were watching you, controlling you, or plotting against you?\n\nPatient: I don’t know… I don’t think so, not like hearing somebody talking to me when nobody’s there. I mean, sometimes in an old house you hear a creak or the refrigerator hums or there’s a car outside, and I might look around, but I don’t think that’s what you mean.\n\nAs far as people watching me or plotting, well… I do feel people looking at me when I’m doing those odd things at church, because they are looking, you know? I haven’t had anybody say, “You’re shaking,” or “You’re walking funny,” not that I remember. And with bladder control, no, I can’t think of any new trouble there around the same time.\n\nIf there’s something small happening, maybe I’m missing it, because I’m usually more worried about when I freeze up or when people are looking at me strange. But no, nothing physical like that really stands out to me.\n\nDoctor: Before these last six months, had you ever experienced anything like this—odd thinking, unusual behavior, or being told your thoughts didn't make sense—earlier in your life, even many years ago?\n\nPatient: Before that? I don’t really think so… not like this. I mean, I’ve always been a person who can talk around a thing, my children would probably tell you that, and I never had much schooling, so sometimes I don’t have the right words quick. But this change, the way people started looking at me funny and me getting mixed up more, that feels like it began after my closest choir friend died.\n\nThat was… let me think… about 11 months ago now. I don’t know if I noticed it right away, but looking back, that’s when I started feeling different, and I think that’s when others began noticing I wasn’t quite myself.\n\nSo no, I wouldn’t say this was happening all through my life. It’s more since she passed, about 11 months ago.\n\nDoctor: Over the past several months, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, like church activities or time with family, along with any changes in your appetite or sleep?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I still care about church and my family, if that’s what you mean. I don’t feel like I just stopped loving those things. But sometimes I don’t feel as eager to go and do as much, especially if I think I might get mixed up or people might notice me not answering right.\n\nSo I don’t know if that’s losing pleasure exactly, or if it’s more that I get nervous and tired thinking about it. I’ve never had somebody tell me I was shaking or out of it that way. And fainting… no, I don’t think I’ve passed out. I’ll start about the blankets, then somehow I’m talking about beans from the potluck, then a hymn we used to sing, then my roses at home, and I can see on their faces they’re trying to follow me but they can’t find what I’m saying.\n\nIt’s not that I’m trying to be difficult. But other days, especially when I feel put on the spot, I just can’t seem to stay on the one thing they asked.\n\nDoctor: \n\nPatient: Yes… that’s the trouble I notice. When the ladies at church ask me something simple, like whether the blankets are in the closet or if I’m coming to choir practice, I really do mean to answer them plain. I know what they asked me, at least at first.\n\nBut then once I start talking, it’s like my words take a side road. I’ll begin with the blankets, and then somehow I’m talking about the beans from the potluck, and then that reminds me of a hymn, and then I’m saying something about my roses at home. In my mind it feels tied together somehow, like one thing leads to the next, but I can see by their faces that they’re not following me.\n\nThey’ll just look at me kind of puzzled, like they can’t find the point of what I’m saying. And then I get embarrassed, because I wasn’t trying to wander all over. I was only trying to answer the question.\n\nDoctor: Have your family noticed you having more trouble than before managing everyday tasks—like cooking, handling money, or keeping track of appointments—separate from the times you freeze up or get tangled in your words?\n\nPatient: Yes… my family has noticed some, mostly around my church things. I don’t do as much as I used to, and that bothers me because church was where I felt useful.\n\nI used to help more with choir and little volunteer jobs, like keeping track of who was supposed to bring what, or setting things out, or making sure something got passed to the right person. But lately I’ll mix up the plans, or I’ll tell one lady the wrong thing, or I’ll think I already handled something and then it turns out somebody else has to go back and fix it.\n\nIt’s not every single thing, and I’m still trying, but I’ve had to step back some. People get uncomfortable, I can tell. They don’t always say it mean, but they’ll kind of take the paper from me or say, “That’s all right, I’ll do it,” and then I feel like I’ve made more work for them. So I’m not leading or helping with choir and volunteering the way I used to. My family sees that, and they know it’s not like me.\n\nDoctor: Have you or your family noticed times when you seem confused about what day it is, where you are, or who the people around you are?\n\nPatient: No… I don’t think so. Not like that.\n\nI mean, I might lose track of what I was doing in the middle of something, or I might have to think a minute what day choir practice is, but I don’t usually forget where I am or who people are. At church I know I’m at church, and I know the ladies there. I know my family when they come around.\n\nSometimes if I’m tired or somebody asks me too many things at once, I can feel mixed up, but it’s more like I need a minute to gather myself. I haven’t had anybody say, “You don’t know where you are,” or anything like that. At least… not that I know of.\n\nDoctor: During one of these freezing spells, if someone gently moved your arm or hand into a new position, would it stay there on its own for a while, as if you were holding it that way?\n\nPatient: I… I don’t rightly know if my arm would stay exactly like that if someone moved it. I don’t think anyone has tried to put my hand somewhere and see. Or if they did, I may not have noticed it that way.\n\nWhat I can say is, that’s sort of why I came in, Doctor. At church I keep doing these odd things, and it embarrasses me afterward. Like I’ll be standing by the potluck table with the serving spoon lifted up, just holding it there, and people are waiting for me to scoop the food or pass it along, and I’m just… stopped. Not doing anything. And then someone will say my name, or touch my elbow, and I realize I’ve been standing there looking foolish.\n\nAnd another time I was folding napkins, the same stack, over and over. I thought I was helping, but I was just doing it again and again while the ladies were waiting on me to finish. So with the arm thing, I’m not sure about the exact way you mean, but I do get stuck in positions or actions like that, and it’s not on purpose.\n\nDoctor: Thinking back over these past several months, would you say your confusion and trouble managing things at church have been getting a little worse each month, or have they stayed about the same since they first started?\n\nPatient: I think… it’s hard for me to say if it’s worse every month, like in a straight line. It hasn’t been like one day I was fine and then the next month I couldn’t do anything. But it has gotten to where I’ve had to step back more than I wanted to.\n\nAt church, especially with choir things and the little volunteer jobs, I used to be trusted with keeping track of plans, who was bringing what, what needed to be set out, who needed to be told something. And now I mix those things up. I’ll think I told the right person and then find out I told somebody else, or I’ll believe I handled something and then someone has to go back behind me and fix it.\n\nSo whether it’s getting worse month by month… I don’t know exactly. And I’ve had to stop doing as much with choir and volunteering because I don’t want to make more trouble for everybody. That’s been the big change.\n\nDoctor: Do these freezing spells and repeated movements ever happen at times when your mind feels clear and you’re not having trouble finding your words, or do they only occur when you’re already feeling confused or tangled up in your thoughts?\n\nPatient: It can happen even when I think I’m all right, Doctor. Sometimes I feel embarrassed after, because they saw it before I did.\n\nSo I don’t know if my mind is ever completely clear the way you mean, but these odd things don’t only happen when I already know I’m confused. But this change, the way people started looking at me funny and me getting mixed up more, that feels like it began after my closest choir friend died.\n\nThat was… let me think… about 11 months ago now. It still feels recent some days, because she and I sat together so many years, and when she was gone it was like the whole row at church changed. I don’t know if I noticed it right away, but looking back, that’s when I started feeling different, and I think that’s when others began noticing I wasn’t quite myself.\n\nSo no, I wouldn’t say this was happening all through my life. It’s more since she passed, about 11 months ago.\n\nDoctor: Over the past several months, have you noticed a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, like church activities or time with family, along with any changes in your appetite or sleep?\n\nPatient: I’m not sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I still care about church and my family, if that’s what you mean. I don’t feel like I just stopped loving those things. But sometimes I don’t feel as eager to go and do as much, especially if I think I might get mixed up or people might notice me not answering right.\n\nSo I don’t know if that’s losing pleasure exactly, or if it’s more that I get nervous and tired thinking about it.
